// purpose: demo-app - "Lumen Supply" (AAP 0.7.1 Group 5). The Next.js 16.3.5 App Router application this repository instruments. It is an ordinary application workspace and depends on none of the product packages, so this project declares no project `references` at all: nothing here imports a workspace package or a tracing library, and instrumentation reaches it at runtime (browser agent, Node preload) or through a recorded, reversible patch - never through a compile-time dependency.
// requirements: Three sets of requirements meet in this file, and the notes below say which option serves which, because a few of them look redundant otherwise: (A) The root solution build. The root tsconfig.json references this project and `pnpm typecheck` is `pnpm demo:generate && tsc -b`, so the project must be `composite` and must emit its declarations outside every tracked directory of the worktree. (B) tsconfig.base.json, which carries the repository's strictness, language level and declaration-emit conventions. Only what Next.js needs is overridden here. (C) Next.js itself.
// requirements.next: (C) `next dev` and `next build` call writeConfigurationDefaults(), which rewrites tsconfig.json in place - except that it returns before writing anything when the raw file contains `extends` or `references` ("Bail automatic setup when the user has extended or referenced another config", next/dist/lib/typescript/writeConfigurationDefaults.js in next@16.3.5). The `extends` below is therefore what keeps this file byte-stable across dev and build runs, which matters because a rewritten tsconfig.json would leave `git status --porcelain -- apps/demo-app` dirty and fail the `residual-worktree` rule of `pnpm check:no-residual-instrumentation`.
// requirements.next-restated: (C) Every option Next.js manages is nevertheless restated verbatim, so the rewrite would still be a no-op if that bail ever disappeared: Next compares its required values against the *raw* file and does not resolve `extends`, and it writes its suggested values whenever the key is merely absent. Each such option's note below is marked "(C)".
// format: Strict JSON, like tsconfig.base.json, the root tsconfig.json and every other tsconfig in this repository: both a JSONC-aware reader (`ts.readConfigFile`, and the comment-json reader Next.js uses) and a bare `JSON.parse` read this file, so no tool reading it has to know which one to reach for - tsc, ESLint, Prettier, Next.js and Vitest would all accept comments in a tsconfig, but nothing that reads this one has to. The rationale therefore lives in the `"// …"` string keys of this object rather than in comments; they are unknown top-level keys, which TypeScript ignores and which writeConfigurationDefaults() neither requires nor suggests, so they change nothing about the bail described above. A `"// …"` key inside `compilerOptions` would be a hard error instead (TS5023, "Unknown compiler option"), so every note about a single option lives up here under a `"// compilerOptions.<option>"` key and never beside the option itself.
// compilerOptions.composite: Solution build and declaration emit (A). Inherited from the base and restated because this project is referenced by the root solution file: `tsc -b` refuses to build a referenced project that is not composite.
// compilerOptions.incremental: (C) Suggested by Next.js when absent; the value it would write is the one the base already sets.
// compilerOptions.noEmit: (C) `noEmit` is stated explicitly, and false, for two reasons. Next.js suggests `noEmit: true` whenever the key is missing, and a composite project with emit disabled contributes no declarations to the solution build (TypeScript 6.0.3 accepts the combination and silently writes only the .tsbuildinfo stamp, which would make this project's participation in `tsc -b` meaningless). Shipping output comes from `next build`; `tsc -b` exists here only as the typecheck gate, so `emitDeclarationOnly`, `declaration` and `declarationMap` below keep it emitting types and nothing else.
// compilerOptions.outDir: The base's `${configDir}` convention, which resolves against *this* directory: everything the gate emits - declarations, declaration maps and the `tsBuildInfoFile` stamp - lands in apps/demo-app/.tsbuild, which .gitignore, .prettierignore and eslint.config.js all ignore. It must never be an output inside app/, src/ or prisma/, because emitted declarations there would show up in `git status` for the demo app.
// compilerOptions.target: Language level and module system (B, restated for C). (C) Next.js suggests ES2017 when `target` is absent; ES2023 is the repository-wide level and Next's SWC pipeline downlevels for browsers on its own.
// compilerOptions.lib: (C) The base ships ["ES2023"] alone so that a Node-only package cannot reach for `window`. This workspace renders in a browser - client components, providers and hooks use the DOM, `fetch` and `performance` - so the DOM libraries are added here. Next.js suggests ["dom", "dom.iterable", "esnext"]; ES2023 is that same ES level pinned to the repository's target.
// compilerOptions.module: (C) Required by Next.js "for dynamic import() support"; already the base's value.
// compilerOptions.moduleResolution: (C) Required by Next.js "to match modern bundler resolution"; already the base's value.
// compilerOptions.esModuleInterop: (C) Required by Next.js as a "requirement for SWC / babel".
// compilerOptions.resolveJsonModule: (C) Required by Next.js "to match webpack resolution".
// compilerOptions.verbatimModuleSyntax: (C) Next.js drops its `isolatedModules` requirement when `verbatimModuleSyntax` is true in the raw file, and requires `isolatedModules` otherwise. Both are stated, so either branch matches. Practically it means `import type` / `export type` are mandatory in this workspace, exactly as everywhere else in the repository.
// compilerOptions.jsx: (C) Next 16.3.5 *requires* "react-jsx": getDesiredCompilerOptions() sets `jsx: { parsedValue: 'react-jsx', value: 'react-jsx', reason: 'next.js uses the React automatic runtime' }`, and would overwrite anything else - "preserve" was the required value of earlier majors only. It is also the base's value, so .tsx files here need no `import React`.
// compilerOptions.allowJs: (C) Next.js suggests `allowJs: true` when the key is absent. The demo is TypeScript only, like the rest of the repository, and stating the base's value keeps that decision in this file rather than relying on a suggested default.
// compilerOptions.strict: (C) Next.js suggests `strict: false` when the key is absent; the demo app is held to the same strictness as the product. `strictNullChecks` is implied by `strict` and restated because Next.js writes it separately for projects that are not strict.
// compilerOptions.skipLibCheck: (C) Suggested by Next.js when absent; already the base's value. Third party declarations - Next, React, Prisma, pg - are not this repository's to fix. Note that it does not cover the generated Prisma client, which the `prisma-client` generator emits as TypeScript *sources*: those are checked as first-party code, and they pass the base's strict set as generated (verified against Prisma 7.10.0 output), so no strictness flag is relaxed for them here.
// compilerOptions.plugins: Editor integration. (C) Next.js adds this entry when it is missing. `tsc` ignores `plugins`; it enables the Next.js language-service plugin in the editor, which flags invalid Server/Client Component boundaries while the demo is authored.
// compilerOptions.types: Ambient types. The base deliberately leaves `types` unset so each workspace declares its own ambient packages. This one needs Node (next.config.ts, prisma.config.ts, prisma/seed.ts, the pg pool and the generated Prisma client all use `node:` built-ins and `process.env`) plus the React typings. Listing them keeps unrelated globals hoisted elsewhere in the monorepo - Chrome, VS Code, Vitest - out of this program. Module imports that resolve through @types (for example `pg` via @types/pg) are unaffected by this list, and the triple-slash references inside the generated next-env.d.ts still pull in Next's own ambient types.
// compilerOptions.paths: The single path alias. `@/...` maps to this workspace's src/ tree, so app/** and src/** import `@/components/...`, `@/providers/...`, `@/hooks/...`, `@/lib/...`, `@/server/...` and `@/generated/prisma/client`. It is deliberately the only alias in the workspace.
// compilerOptions.paths.baseUrl: `baseUrl` is NOT set, and must not be: TypeScript 6.0.3 answers it with "error TS5101: Option 'baseUrl' is deprecated and will stop functioning in TypeScript 7.0", which fails `tsc -b` outright. `paths` alone is enough - TypeScript resolves the values below against the directory of the config that declares them, and Next.js resolves them the same way (build/load-jsconfig.js falls back to `pathsBasePath`, so "baseUrl is not required for path aliases to work in webpack"), which keeps the compiler and the bundler in agreement.
// include: `include` is the set Next.js expects to find, so it has nothing to add: next-env.d.ts is generated by Next.js and git-ignored, therefore absent on a clean clone. It belongs in `include`, never in `files`: a `files` entry that does not exist is a hard error, while an `include` glob that matches nothing is ignored. Nothing in the demo may depend on what it declares (in particular, no static image imports - use `next/image` with a string `src` into public/), so `pnpm typecheck` succeeds on a fresh clone that has never run a build. **/*.ts and **/*.tsx cover app/**, src/**, next.config.ts, prisma.config.ts and prisma/seed.ts, so the configuration and seed scripts are checked too.
// include.next-types: The two .next globs: getTypeDefinitionGlobPatterns() asks for `<distDir>/types/**/*.ts` plus its dev counterpart, and distDir is .next for `next build` and .next/dev for `next dev`. Listing both means Next.js never appends a glob (which would rewrite this file) and the generated route types - the typed-routes unions and the validator that checks every page, layout and route-handler signature - are visible to whichever mode produced them. They are git-ignored, so they cannot dirty the worktree either. The two generated routes.d.ts copies declare the same ambient names; `skipLibCheck` above is what keeps that from being a duplicate-identifier error, and a `.next` left over from a route that no longer exists is cleared by deleting the directory.
// exclude: Declaring `exclude` replaces the base's list, which is why .tsbuild is repeated here: TypeScript excludes `outDir` automatically only when `exclude` is absent, so without this entry the declarations emitted by `tsc -b` would become inputs of the next run. `node_modules` is the value Next.js writes when `exclude` is missing. `.next` as a whole is NOT excluded, because that would also drop the generated route types the `include` globs above deliberately pick up.
